content: 1. Permanent neurological or psychiatric complications can develop in 30–50% of individuals who contract encephalitis. There is currently no cure for this disease. Treatment is primarily aimed at alleviating severe clinical symptoms and supporting the patient in overcoming the infection. Safe and effective vaccines are available to prevent Japanese encephalitis. 2. West Nile Virus (WNV) is a member of the Flavivirus genus and is part of the Japanese encephalitis antigenic complex within the Flaviviridae family. WNV can cause neurological disease and death, although approximately 80% of infected individuals remain asymptomatic. The virus is commonly found in Africa, Europe, the Middle East, North America, and West Asia. It is maintained in nature through a transmission cycle involving birds and mosquitoes. Humans, horses, and other mammals can also become infected. WNV is primarily transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. In horses, the virus can cause severe disease and death. Vaccines are available for horses but not yet for humans. 3. Meningitis is a clinical syndrome characterized by inflammation of the meninges, most commonly caused by infectious agents such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa. Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and remains a significant public health challenge, particularly in resource-limited settings. The most common causes of community-acquired acute bacterial meningitis are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. In newborns, Streptococcus agalactiae is the leading causative agent. Acute bacterial meningitis can present as either sporadic or epidemic disease, depending on the causative agent and geographical context. For example, N. meningitidis is a human pathogen transmitted via respiratory droplets, responsible for recurrent epidemics in the African meningitis belt during the dry season, as well as sporadic cases and small outbreaks in other temperate and subtropical regions. Safe and effective vaccines are available to prevent the primary causes of acute bacterial meningitis. 4. Seizures occur due to excessive electrical discharges in a group of brain cells. These discharges can originate in different parts of the brain. Seizures can range from brief lapses in attention or muscle jerks to severe and prolonged convulsions. Their frequency can vary from less than one per year to several per day. Common triggers include changes in sleep patterns, jet lag, sleep deprivation, travel, and alcohol or drug use. Travelers with a history of seizures should carry sufficient medication in their hand luggage to account for unexpected travel diversions or lost luggage. It is essential to take medications as prescribed, as missing a dose can lead to a seizure. Travelers are also advised to carry abortive anti-seizure medications, though some of these may be controlled substances in certain countries. 5. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is a rare condition in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves. It can affect individuals of all ages but is more common in adults and males. Most people recover fully, even from severe cases, but in rare instances, GBS can lead to near-total paralysis and breathing difficulties, making it potentially life-threatening. Initial symptoms include weakness or tingling sensations, typically starting in the legs and spreading to the arms and face. In some cases, these symptoms progress to ascending paralysis. Approximately one-third of individuals experience chest muscle involvement, leading to breathing difficulties. Prompt treatment and monitoring are critical, and some patients may require intensive care. Treatment includes supportive care and immunological therapies. 6. Stroke is the leading cause of disability worldwide and the second leading cause of death. High blood pressure is a major clinical risk factor, along with tobacco use, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, alcohol consumption, atrial fibrillation, elevated blood lipid levels, obesity, genetic predisposition, stress, and depression. Stroke survivors may experience physical disability, communication difficulties, and loss of work, income, and social connections. Key signs of stroke include facial drooping, arm weakness on one side, and speech difficulties, such as slurring or nonsensical speech. Other symptoms may include vision changes, loss of balance, or dizziness. Recognizing these signs and seeking immediate emergency medical care can save lives and improve outcomes for survivors. 7. Migraine typically begins at puberty and primarily affects individuals aged 35–45 years. It is more common in women, often due to hormonal influences, with a prevalence ratio of approximately 2:1. Migraine is a recurrent, often lifelong condition characterized by attacks of one-sided, pulsating headaches that are aggravated by routine physical activity, noise, and bright lights, and are often accompanied by nausea. Travel can exacerbate migraines due to disruptions in sleep patterns, eating habits, alcohol consumption, and time-zone changes. Travelers should continue taking prophylactic migraine medications and carry sufficient doses of abortive treatments, which are most effective when taken at the onset of symptoms. Some individuals may take a prophylactic NSAID before flying to prevent migraines. Staying adequately hydrated can also help prevent migraines during travel. 8. Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurological condition that impairs movement, mental health, and sleep, and is associated with pain and other health issues. It leads to high rates of disability and care dependency, with many patients also developing dementia. While PD primarily affects older individuals, younger people can also be diagnosed. Men are more frequently affected than women. The most common medication for PD is a combination of levodopa and carbidopa, which increases dopamine levels in the brain. Other medications, such as anticholinergics, may be used to reduce involuntary muscle movements. When traveling, individuals with PD should bring ample supplies of their medications, as these may not be available at their destination. Allowing extra time for travel logistics is advisable, as slower movements may require longer transit times. 9. Dementia is a syndrome caused by various diseases that progressively destroy nerve cells and damage the brain, leading to cognitive impairment beyond what is expected from normal aging. While consciousness remains intact, cognitive decline is often accompanied or preceded by changes in mood, emotional control, behavior, or motivation. Travel can heighten confusion and stress in individuals with dementia due to changes in routine, unfamiliar environments, time-zone shifts, and sleep disturbances, increasing the risk of getting lost, experiencing delirium, or worsening cognitive difficulties. For those with mild to moderate dementia, travel may offer psychosocial benefits, but for those with advanced dementia, the risks may outweigh the benefits. Careful planning and discussion with caregivers are essential. 10. Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) encompass behavioral and cognitive challenges that arise during developmental stages, leading to difficulties in acquiring and performing intellectual, motor, language, or social functions. These disorders include intellectual developmental disorders, developmental speech or language disorders, autism spectrum disorder, developmental learning disorders, developmental motor coordination disorder, and ADHD. Travel can be particularly challenging for individuals with NDDs due to changes in routine, unpredictability, crowds, and sensory overload. Planning ahead, maintaining routines, and bringing items to support self-regulation, such as headphones or sunglasses, can help. Informing travel carriers of specific needs, such as priority boarding or special seating, and allowing extra time for travel can also reduce stress.
